Recent work supports evidence-linked annotation rather than treating every skip as a known recommendation failure. ACUEval (2024) decomposes outputs into atomic claims and checks each against source evidence; AFaCTA (2024) emphasizes verifiability and explicit definitions. A proposed adaptation for this task: label redundancy only with an identified duplicate or explicitly recorded repetition complaint; specification conflict only when documented requirements contradict documented item attributes; unsupported assumption when a rationale asserts unobserved ownership, needs, or specifications; insufficient relevance evidence when available histories and metadata cannot justify relevance. Missing specifications remain unknown, and a skip alone establishes no cause. This four-part rubric is a task-specific synthesis, not a validated taxonomy from these papers. [ACUEval](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.597/), [AFaCTA](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.104/).

Annotation research finds that task wording and annotator choice change instance-level judgments, while selective annotation research supports routing difficult cases to experts. For the twenty feedback users, independently double-annotate available recommendation–feedback pairs, retain evidence spans and unknown labels, and adjudicate disagreements after measuring agreement. Report label counts, raw agreement, chance-corrected agreement, abstention coverage, and errors among decided cases; uncertainty should reflect clustering by user and the small five-user category samples. These are proposed checks, not measured results. Abstention research motivates evaluating both coverage and error rather than rewarding blanket refusal. Keep this audit separate from inference scoring and retain macro validation HR@10 for model selection. [Disagreement study](https://aclanthology.org/2025.comedi-1.3/), [Selective Annotation](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.17/), [Abstention survey](https://aclanthology.org/2025.tacl-1.26/).
